acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Responsiveness check in the primary assessment
acros.info: Rapid mental-status scale used at the start of the primary assessment, before the ABCs.

mcs.stem: AVPU is used during which assessment phase?
wrong: The secondary exam comes after AVPU has been established.
Reassessment repeats findings, it does not begin them.
Scene size-up happens before patient contact.
mcs.why: AVPU is the quick responsiveness check at the start of the primary assessment.

mcs.stem: In the primary assessment, which acronym follows AVPU?
wrong: SAMPLE is history taking, after the primary.
OPQRST expands the chief complaint during history.
DCAP-BTLS belongs to the secondary trauma exam.
mcs.why: After establishing responsiveness with AVPU, the primary assessment moves to Airway, Breathing, Circulation.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Primary assessment priorities
acros.info: The life-threat priorities of the primary assessment. Some curricula add X (exsanguinating hemorrhage) before A.

mcs.stem: In XABC, what does the X stand for?
wrong: Fractures are a secondary-exam concern.
Exposure is part of the trauma exam, not the X.
Oxygen falls under breathing support.
mcs.why: X puts control of exsanguinating (life-threatening) hemorrhage before the airway when massive bleeding is present.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: History-taking mnemonic
letters: Events leading up to the illness or injury
acros.info: Structured patient history gathered after the primary assessment; OPQRST expands the S when the complaint is pain.

mcs.stem: When is the SAMPLE history obtained?
wrong: Responsiveness (AVPU) always comes first.
Size-up precedes any patient questioning.
History starts on scene when the patient is stable enough.
mcs.why: SAMPLE is gathered during history taking, after life threats are addressed in the primary assessment.

mcs.stem: Which acronym expands the S of SAMPLE for a pain complaint?
wrong: DCAP-BTLS lists physical exam findings.
AEIOU-TIPS lists altered mental status causes.
AVPU grades responsiveness.
mcs.why: OPQRST explores a pain or symptom complaint in depth — the detailed version of signs and symptoms.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Pain and symptom exploration
acros.info: Deepens the chief complaint — typically asked with the history in a responsive medical patient.

mcs.stem: OPQRST is primarily used to explore what?
wrong: MOI is judged during scene size-up.
Vitals are measured, not interviewed.
Medications are the M of SAMPLE.
mcs.why: OPQRST characterizes the chief complaint — classically pain — through onset, provocation, quality, region, severity, and time.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Trauma exam findings
acros.info: What you look and feel for on each body region during the rapid trauma / secondary assessment.

mcs.stem: During which phase is DCAP-BTLS applied?
wrong: Size-up assesses scene safety and MOI.
The primary targets immediate life threats.
SAMPLE is verbal history, not palpation.
mcs.why: DCAP-BTLS structures the head-to-toe inspection and palpation during the rapid trauma / secondary exam.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Causes of altered mental status
acros.info: Differential checklist for the patient with altered mental status.

mcs.stem: AEIOU-TIPS helps generate a differential for what presentation?
wrong: Chest pain uses OPQRST exploration.
Distress is assessed with breathing parameters.
Trauma findings follow DCAP-BTLS.
mcs.why: Each letter is a reversible or treatable cause of altered mental status to consider.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Pupil examination
acros.info: Documents a normal pupil exam; unequal or fixed pupils suggest neurologic compromise.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Quantified consciousness score
acros.info: Scores Eye opening (max 4), Verbal (max 5), Motor (max 6); total 3–15.

mcs.stem: What are the three components scored by the GCS?
wrong: Those are vital sign checks, not GCS.
Those are the primary assessment priorities.
Those belong to a stroke or cerebellar exam.
mcs.why: GCS totals eye opening (4), verbal response (5), and motor response (6) — a maximum of 15.

mcs.stem: What is the maximum GCS score?
wrong: The components sum to more than 10.
Component maximums are 4, 5, and 6.
12 is a possible score, not the ceiling.
mcs.why: 4 (eye) + 5 (verbal) + 6 (motor) = 15; the minimum is 3.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Trauma cause evaluated at size-up
acros.info: Judged during scene size-up for trauma patients; the medical counterpart is NOI, nature of illness.

mcs.stem: When is the MOI first evaluated?
wrong: The secondary exam uses MOI already known.
History refines it; size-up establishes it.
Reassessment tracks changes, not causes.
mcs.why: Mechanism of injury is read from the scene itself, before patient contact — the medical parallel is NOI.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Medical cause evaluated at size-up
acros.info: The medical patient's counterpart to MOI — what appears to be wrong, judged from scene and bystanders.

acros.subject: Patient Assessment
acros.name: Distal extremity check
acros.info: Checked distal to any extremity injury, before and after splinting.

mcs.stem: When must CSM be rechecked?
wrong: A single check misses splint-induced compromise.
Deficits can be painless.
The comparison across the intervention is the point.
mcs.why: Circulation, sensation, and movement are assessed distal to injury both before and after immobilization.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Difficult airway prediction
acros.info: Predicts a difficult intubation: external features, 3-3-2 rule, Mallampati class (needs an upright cooperative patient), obstructions, and neck mobility.

mcs.stem: What does LEMON predict?
wrong: Secretions and gag status guide suctioning.
SpO2 and capnography quantify oxygenation.
Settings come after the airway is secured.
mcs.why: LEMON structures the difficult-airway assessment before an intubation attempt.

mcs.stem: In the 3-3-2 rule, the '2' is the distance between which landmarks?
options: The chin and the hyoid bone
wrong: Chin-to-hyoid is the second 3 (mandible).
Incisor gap is the first 3 (mouth opening).
The sternum is not part of 3-3-2.
mcs.why: Mouth opening 3 fingers, mandible length 3 fingers, hyoid-to-thyroid-notch 2 fingers.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Drug-assisted intubation sequence
acros.info: Prepare → preoxygenate → premedicate → sedate then paralyze → intubate → maintain. Adequate paralysis: apnea, slack mandible, lost eyelash reflex.

mcs.stem: In RSI, which comes first: sedation or paralysis?
wrong: Paralyzing an aware patient leaves them conscious and immobile.
They are given sequentially.
The order is fixed for patient protection.
mcs.why: Sedate as soon as hemodynamically appropriate, then paralyze — paralytics have no effect on consciousness.

mcs.stem: After succinylcholine RSI, paralysis is maintained with what?
wrong: Redosing the depolarizer is not the maintenance strategy.
Sedation does not sustain paralysis.
Succinylcholine wears off in 5–10 minutes.
mcs.why: Succinylcholine is short-acting; a nondepolarizer (vecuronium, rocuronium, pancuronium) maintains paralysis once placement is certain.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Noninvasive ventilatory support
acros.info: Opens collapsed alveoli, pushes O2 across the membrane, forces interstitial fluid back into circulation. Requires an alert patient following commands; PEEP 5–10 cm H2O.

mcs.stem: Which patient is CPAP appropriate for?
options: Actively vomiting with a GI bleed
wrong: Inability to follow commands contraindicates it.
Hypotension and chest trauma contraindicate it.
GI bleeding and vomiting contraindicate it.
mcs.why: CPAP demands an alert cooperative patient — typical thresholds: rate over 26/min and SpO2 under 90%.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Expiratory resistance pressure
acros.info: The resistance the patient exhales against during CPAP; therapeutic range 5–10 cm H2O.

mcs.stem: What is the general therapeutic PEEP range?
wrong: That is above the general range.
That is subtherapeutic.
That risks serious barotrauma.
mcs.why: 5–10 cm H2O, set manually by manometer or by a fixed valve.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Choking emergency
acros.info: Mild: patient coughs — leave alone and monitor. Severe: abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts if pregnant/obese); unresponsive → compressions.

mcs.stem: A responsive FBAO patient with a strong cough gets what care?
wrong: Thrusts are for severe obstruction.
Blind sweeps risk pushing the object deeper.
They are moving air on their own.
mcs.why: A forceful cough is the most effective dislodging mechanism — intervene only if the obstruction becomes severe.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Oral airway adjunct
acros.info: Curved device holding the tongue off the glottis. Only for unresponsive patients with no gag reflex; sized mouth-corner to earlobe.

mcs.stem: The OPA is contraindicated in which patient?
options: Anyone with an intact gag reflex
Patients who need a bite block
wrong: That is exactly its indication.
It facilitates bag-mask ventilation.
It doubles as a bite block.
mcs.why: An intact gag means gagging, retching, and vomiting — remove immediately if the patient gags.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Nasal airway adjunct
acros.info: Soft tube through the nose; tolerated with an intact gag. Contraindicated in nose trauma or suspected skull fracture.

mcs.stem: Which finding bars the NPA?
wrong: The NPA is the adjunct of choice with a gag.
A closed mouth is no obstacle to nasal insertion.
Altered LOC with a gag is its indication.
mcs.why: Nose trauma or possible skull fracture contraindicates the NPA.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Supraglottic rescue airway
acros.info: Cuff seals around the laryngeal inlet. Main disadvantage: no aspiration protection. Less effective in obesity, pregnancy, high pulmonary pressures.

mcs.stem: What is the LMA's main disadvantage?
options: It cannot attach to a bag device
wrong: No laryngoscopy is one of its advantages.
Its standard adapter fits any ventilation device.
It causes less trauma than intubation.
mcs.why: The LMA does not protect against aspiration — its most significant limitation.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Definitive airway tube
acros.info: Passed through the glottis, cuff sealed against the tracheal wall (5–10 mL). Murphy's eye ventilates past an occluded tip; adult sizes to 9.0 mm.

mcs.stem: What is the first and most reliable confirmation of ETT placement?
options: Seeing it pass through the cords
wrong: Auscultation is the second step.
Colorimetric detectors are temporary adjuncts.
Chest rise supports but does not prove placement.
mcs.why: Direct visualization of the tube passing the vocal cords, then auscultation, with continuous waveform capnography as the most reliable ongoing monitor.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Placement-check device
acros.info: Bulb model: brisk expansion = trachea; stays collapsed = esophagus. Backup when waveform capnography is unavailable.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Chronic obstructive disease
acros.info: Air-trapping disease; early inspiratory crackles are common, and the I/E ratio stretches toward 1:4–1:5 in obstruction.

acros.subject: Airway & Respiratory
acros.name: Manual ventilation device
acros.info: Adult bag 1,200–1,600 mL; deliver 500–600 mL (6–7 mL/kg) over 1 s. Adults every 5–6 s, peds every 3–5 s, arrest every 6–8 s.

mcs.stem: How much volume does each adult BVM breath deliver?
wrong: Emptying the bag overinflates and distends the stomach.
That is the infant bag capacity.
That is the bag's total capacity, not the delivered volume.
mcs.why: 500–600 mL (6–7 mL/kg) over one second — judged by visible chest rise.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: The heart's pacemaker
acros.info: Primary pacemaker in the right atrial wall; sets the intrinsic heart rate.

mcs.stem: What is the role of the SA node?
wrong: The AV node provides the delay.
Chambers pump; nodes conduct.
Baroreceptors sense pressure.
mcs.why: The sinoatrial node initiates the heartbeat; the AV node relays and delays the impulse to the ventricles.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: Conduction relay node
acros.info: Delays each impulse so the atria finish contracting before the ventricles fire.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: Oxygen-carrying cell
acros.info: Carries hemoglobin; anemia or blood loss reduces oxygen-carrying capacity.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: Immune defense cell
acros.info: The blood's immune defenders; counts rise with infection.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: Cardiac output
acros.info: Cardiac output = stroke volume × pulse rate. Positive pressure ventilation reduces it by cutting venous return.

mcs.stem: Cardiac output equals stroke volume multiplied by what?
wrong: Pressure is a product of output and resistance.
Breathing does not enter the formula.
Resistance relates output to pressure, not defines output.
mcs.why: CO = SV × pulse rate — why excessive intrathoracic pressure from PPV, which cuts venous return and stroke volume, drops output.

acros.subject: Circulatory
acros.name: Blood pressure
acros.info: Systolic over diastolic; a systolic drop >10 mm Hg on inhalation is pulsus paradoxus.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Central nervous system
acros.info: Brain and spinal cord — the processing core the PNS reports to.

mcs.stem: What structures make up the CNS?
wrong: Peripheral nerves form the PNS.
Cranial nerves are peripheral once they exit.
Ganglia belong to the autonomic PNS.
mcs.why: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; everything else is the peripheral nervous system.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Peripheral nervous system
acros.info: All nervous tissue outside brain and cord — cranial nerves, spinal nerves, autonomic fibers.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Autonomic nervous system
acros.info: Involuntary control — sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) divisions.

mcs.stem: What are the two divisions of the ANS?
wrong: Somatic is the voluntary system, apart from the ANS.
Those divide the nervous system as a whole.
Those describe signal direction, not ANS divisions.
mcs.why: Sympathetic drives fight-or-flight; parasympathetic drives rest-and-digest.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Cerebrospinal fluid
acros.info: Cushions brain and cord and buffers pressure changes; leaks from ears or nose suggest skull fracture.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Intracranial pressure
acros.info: Pressure inside the skull; etomidate is favored for induction partly because it spares ICP.

mcs.stem: Which induction agent has little effect on ICP?
wrong: Ketamine is chosen for hypotension, not ICP neutrality.
Midazolam is not the ICP-sparing induction choice.
Fentanyl is an analgesic premedication.
mcs.why: Etomidate is fast, short, and spares pulse, blood pressure, and intracranial pressure.

acros.subject: Nervous System
acros.name: Level of consciousness
acros.info: Graded with AVPU or GCS. Paralytics do not affect it — the paralyzed patient can still hear, feel, and think.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Water-retention hormone
acros.info: From the posterior pituitary; makes the kidneys reabsorb water, concentrating urine.

mcs.stem: What does ADH cause the kidneys to do?
wrong: Aldosterone governs sodium handling.
EPO release is a separate renal response to hypoxia.
Glucose filtration is not ADH's action.
mcs.why: Antidiuretic hormone promotes water reabsorption, reducing urine output and conserving volume.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Thyroid-stimulating hormone
acros.info: Anterior pituitary hormone driving thyroid hormone release, which sets metabolic rate.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Adrenal-stimulating hormone
acros.info: Anterior pituitary hormone driving cortisol release from the adrenal cortex.

mcs.stem: ACTH stimulates which gland?
wrong: TSH targets the thyroid.
Insulin and glucagon come from pancreatic islets.
The pineal secretes melatonin.
mcs.why: Adrenocorticotropic hormone drives the adrenal cortex to release cortisol.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Gamete-development hormone
acros.info: Anterior pituitary gonadotropin: matures ovarian follicles and drives sperm production.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Ovulation trigger
acros.info: Its surge triggers ovulation; in males it drives testosterone production.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Growth hormone
acros.info: Anterior pituitary hormone promoting tissue growth and protein synthesis.

acros.subject: Endocrine
acros.name: Calcium-raising hormone
acros.info: Raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney, and gut absorption.

mcs.stem: What does PTH do to blood calcium?
wrong: Calcitonin is the calcium-lowering hormone.
Calcium regulation is its entire role.
Protein binding is not a PTH action.
mcs.why: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium; calcitonin opposes it.

acros.subject: Cells & Metabolism
acros.name: Cellular energy currency
acros.info: The cell's energy currency; without oxygen, anaerobic metabolism yields far less ATP plus lactic acid.

mcs.stem: What happens to ATP production without oxygen?
options: It falls, with lactic acid buildup
It rises to compensate for the hypoxia
It stops entirely within a few seconds
wrong: Glycolysis alone yields only a small fraction of aerobic ATP.
Hypoxia cannot be out-produced anaerobically.
A trickle of anaerobic ATP continues, briefly.
mcs.why: Anaerobic metabolism produces far less ATP and accumulates lactic acid — the cellular story behind hypoxia and shock.

acros.subject: Cells & Metabolism
acros.name: Genetic blueprint
acros.info: Double-stranded genetic archive in the nucleus; RNA carries its instructions out for protein synthesis.

acros.subject: Cells & Metabolism
acros.name: Protein-synthesis messenger
acros.info: Single-stranded; messenger RNA ferries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosomes.

acros.subject: Cells & Metabolism
acros.name: Body mass index
acros.info: Weight relative to height squared — a screening measure of body composition, not a direct fat measurement.

acros.subject: Cells & Metabolism
acros.name: Kidney filtration rate
acros.info: Volume filtered by the glomeruli per minute — the core measure of kidney function.

mcs.stem: GFR measures the function of which structure?
wrong: The liver is not a filtration-rate organ in this sense.
Alveoli exchange gases, measured by capnography.
Pancreatic flow is not the GFR.
mcs.why: Glomerular filtration rate quantifies how much plasma the kidney's glomeruli filter per minute.
